results.proposed_proof:
**Given:** Positive reals $I_1<I_2<I_3$, the diagonal map $I$ with $Ie_j=I_je_j$, the field $F(l)=l\times(I^{-1}l)$ on $\mathbb R^3$, and $L\ne0$.

[L1] The system $z'=F(z)$ on the open set $U=\mathbb R^3$ is read as [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] with $D=\mathbb R\times U$; $Le_1$ and $Le_3$ are equilibria exactly when $F(Le_j)=0$, and then Lyapunov stability is the quantified ball statement of [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]].

[L2] The cross product is bilinear and alternating and satisfies $\lVert u\times v\rVert_2\le\lVert u\rVert_2\lVert v\rVert_2$ [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[thm-cross-product-norm-is-the-two-vector-gram-determinant]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

[L3] $F$ is locally Lipschitz in the state variable in the sense of [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]: for $\lVert x\rVert_2,\lVert y\rVert_2\le r$ one has $F(x)-F(y)=(x-y)\times(I^{-1}x)+y\times(I^{-1}(x-y))$ by bilinearity of the cross product [L2], whence $\lVert F(x)-F(y)\rVert_2\le C_r\lVert x-y\rVert_2$ with $C_r:=2\max\{\lVert I^{-1}z\rVert_2:z\in\overline B_r(0)\}$ finite on the compact ball ([[def-metric-ball]], the minimum of $I_j$ gives $\lVert I^{-1}z\rVert_2\le\lVert z\rVert_2/I_1$). Picard-Lindelof therefore applies to the initial value problem of the system [[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]; every datum has a unique maximal solution on an open interval, and every other solution through that datum is a restriction ([[def-maximal-ode-solution]], [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]]).

[L4] Along every solution of $l'=l\times(I^{-1}l)$ the quantities $C(l)=\langle l,l\rangle$ and $E(l)=\tfrac12\langle l,I^{-1}l\rangle$ are constant; for $l=\sum_jl_je_j$ they equal $\sum_jl_j^2$ and $\sum_jl_j^2/(2I_j)$ [[thm-cm-euler-equations-and-torque-free-invariants]].

[L5] Any solution of an autonomous system on $U=\mathbb R^3$ that is trapped near a finite endpoint in a compact subset of $U$ extends past that endpoint: the no-extension hypothesis of [[cor-cm-finite-time-breakdown-requires-escape]] fails under such trapping.

[L6] The Euclidean inner product is bilinear and positive definite, so $\langle u,u\rangle=\lVert u\rVert_2^2$ and $u\ne0$ implies $\lVert u\rVert_2>0$ [[def-inner-product-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].



**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By antisymmetry of the cross product, $F(Le_1)=Le_1\times(L/I_1)e_1=0$ and $F(Le_3)=Le_3\times(L/I_3)e_3=0$, so $Le_1$ and $Le_3$ are equilibria; and [L3] supplies the existence, uniqueness and continuation theory for the system. [given, L1, L2, L3]

1.2 Let $l$ be the maximal solution with prescribed datum at $0$. By [L4] the numbers $C(l(t))=\lVert l(t)\rVert_2^2=\lVert l(0)\rVert_2^2$ and $E(l(t))$ are constant, so the graph of $l$ lies in the compact sphere $\{z:\lVert z\rVert_2=\lVert l(0)\rVert_2\}\subseteq U$. [given, L2, L4]

1.3 Define, for $l=\sum_jl_je_j$, the quantity $D(l):=C(l)/(2I_1)-E(l)=\tfrac12\sum_{j>1}(1/I_1-1/I_j)l_j^2$. Since $1/I_1-1/I_j\ge1/I_1-1/I_2$ for $j=2,3$ by $I_2<I_3$ and $I_1<I_2$, one has $D(l)\ge c(l_2^2+l_3^2)$ with $c:=\tfrac12(1/I_1-1/I_2)>0$. [given, L4, algebra]

2.1 Every maximal solution of the system is defined for all $t\ge0$: if a solution were defined on $[0,b)$ with $0<b<+\infty$ and admitted no extension past $b$, then by step 1.2 it would be trapped in the compact subset $\{z:\lVert z\rVert_2=\lVert l(0)\rVert_2\}$ of $U$ near $b$, and [L5] would give an extension past $b$, a contradiction. [step 1.2, given, L5]

3.1 Let $\varepsilon>0$ and let $c,\kappa:=1/\sqrt{2I_1c}$ be as in step 1.3; choose $\delta>0$ satisfying the finite list of conditions $\delta\le\varepsilon$, $\kappa^2\delta^2\le\varepsilon^2/4$, $\kappa^2\delta^2\le|L|^2/4$, $\delta\le|L|/4$ and $\delta(2|L|+\delta)+\kappa^2\delta^2\le|L|\varepsilon/2$; such a $\delta$ exists because each condition only bounds $\delta$ from above by a positive number. Let $l$ be the maximal solution with $\lVert l(0)-Le_1\rVert_2<\delta$, defined for all $t\ge0$ by step 2.1. Then $l_2(0)^2+l_3(0)^2\le\lVert l(0)-Le_1\rVert_2^2<\delta^2$ and, by [L4] and step 1.3 evaluated at $t=0$, for every $t\ge0$ $$l_2(t)^2+l_3(t)^2\le\frac{D(l(t))}{c}=\frac{D(l(0))}{c}\le\frac{l_2(0)^2+l_3(0)^2}{2I_1c}<\kappa^2\delta^2\le\frac{\varepsilon^2}{4}.$$ [step 2.1, 1.3, given, L4, L6, algebra]

3.2 Combining steps 3.1 and 4.1, $\lVert l(t)-Le_1\rVert_2^2=(l_1(t)-L)^2+l_2(t)^2+l_3(t)^2<\frac{\varepsilon^2}{9}+\frac{\varepsilon^2}{4}<\varepsilon^2$ for all $t\ge0$; since for every $\varepsilon>0$ such a $\delta$ was produced and every maximal solution starting in $B_\delta(Le_1)$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ by step 2.1, $Le_1$ is Lyapunov stable in the sense of [L1]. [step 2.1, 3.1, 4.1, given, L1, algebra]

4.1 With the data of step 3.1: $l_1(t)^2=C(l(0))-l_2(t)^2-l_3(t)^2\ge(|L|-\delta)^2-\kappa^2\delta^2\ge|L|^2/4$ by $\delta\le|L|/4$ and $\kappa^2\delta^2\le|L|^2/4$, so $|l_1(t)|\ge|L|/2$ and $l_1$ has the sign of $L$ (it is continuous, $|l_1|\ge|L|/2$ throughout, and $|l_1(0)-L|<\delta\le|L|/4$). Hence $|l_1(t)+L|\ge3|L|/2$ and $$|l_1(t)-L|=\frac{|l_1(t)^2-L^2|}{|l_1(t)+L|}\le\frac{|C(l(0))-L^2|+l_2(t)^2+l_3(t)^2}{3|L|/2}\le\frac{\delta(2|L|+\delta)+\kappa^2\delta^2}{3|L|/2}\le\frac{\varepsilon}{3}.$$ [step 3.1, given, L4, L6, algebra]

5.1 The same argument with the roles of $e_1$ and $e_3$ exchanged uses $D_3(l):=E(l)-C(l)/(2I_3)=\tfrac12\sum_{j<3}(1/I_j-1/I_3)l_j^2\ge c_3(l_1^2+l_2^2)$ with $c_3:=\tfrac12(1/I_2-1/I_3)>0$, together with the mirrored estimates carrying $(l_1,l_2)$ where steps 1.3, 3.1 and 4.1 carry $(l_2,l_3)$; the certificate $D_3$ is constant along solutions by [L4], so the argument of steps 1.3, 2.1, 3.1, 3.2 and 4.1 applies verbatim to $Le_3$ and proves its Lyapunov stability. [step 1.3, 3.1, 4.1, 3.2, given, L4, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Positive reals $I_1<I_2<I_3$, the diagonal map $I$, the field $F(l)=l\times(I^{-1}l)$ on $U=\mathbb R^3$, and $L\ne0$.

[L1] The system $l'=F(l)$ is read as [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]; $F$ is continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, since for $\lVert x\rVert_2,\lVert y\rVert_2\le r$ one has $F(x)-F(y)=(x-y)\times(I^{-1}x)+y\times(I^{-1}(x-y))$ and hence $\lVert F(x)-F(y)\rVert_2\le C_r\lVert x-y\rVert_2$ for a finite $C_r$; Picard-Lindelof gives local existence and uniqueness, hence a unique maximal solution through every datum ([[def-maximal-ode-solution]], [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]]), and a solution trapped in a compact subset of $U=\mathbb R^3$ near a finite endpoint extends past it [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]], [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], [[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]], [[cor-cm-finite-time-breakdown-requires-escape]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

[L2] Along every solution the invariants $C(l)=\lVert l\rVert_2^2$ and $E(l)=\tfrac12\langle l,I^{-1}l\rangle$ are constant; in the eigenbasis $Ie_j=I_je_j$ one has $C=\sum_jl_j^2$, $E=\sum_jl_j^2/(2I_j)$, and the component equations $l_1'=(1/I_3-1/I_2)l_2l_3$, $l_2'=(1/I_1-1/I_3)l_1l_3$, $l_3'=(1/I_2-1/I_1)l_1l_2$ [[thm-cm-euler-equations-and-torque-free-invariants]].

[L3] The Euler field is even: $F(-l)=(-l)\times(I^{-1}(-l))=F(l)$, by bilinearity and linearity ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]). Put $\sigma:=L/|L|\in\{-1,1\}$, so $\sigma^2=1$ and $L=\sigma|L|$.

[L4] The cross product is bilinear and $\lVert u\times v\rVert_2\le\lVert u\rVert_2\lVert v\rVert_2$; the Euclidean inner product is positive definite [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[thm-cross-product-norm-is-the-two-vector-gram-determinant]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-inner-product-space]].

[L5] If $f:I\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable on an interval with $f'(t)\ge0$ for all interior $t$, then $f$ is nondecreasing; and the product rule $(gh)'=g'h+gh'$ holds; $(e^{\lambda t})'=\lambda e^{\lambda t}$ for real $\lambda$ [[thm-monotonicity-from-the-derivative]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]].



**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 $F(Le_2)=Le_2\times(L/I_2)e_2=0$, so $l_0$ is an equilibrium. Put $\sigma=L/|L|$ as in [L3]. Choose the second and third coordinates of the initial datum with signs $\sigma$ and $-\sigma$, respectively. [given, L1, L3]

2.1 Let $0<\eta_0<\delta_0:=|L|/(2\sqrt{1+a^2})$ and let $0<\eta<\eta_0$. Put $s(\eta):=\sqrt{|L|^2-(1+a^2)\eta^2}>0$ and $l^\eta:=(\eta,\,\sigma s(\eta),\,-\sigma a\eta)$, so that $C(l^\eta)=L^2$ and $E(l^\eta)=L^2/(2I_2)$: indeed $C(l^\eta)=\eta^2+|L|^2-(1+a^2)\eta^2+a^2\eta^2=L^2$ and $E(l^\eta)=\tfrac12\bigl(\eta^2/I_1+(|L|^2-(1+a^2)\eta^2)/I_2+a^2\eta^2/I_3\bigr)=\tfrac12L^2/I_2+\tfrac12\eta^2\bigl(1/I_1-1/I_2-a^2(1/I_2-1/I_3)\bigr)=L^2/(2I_2)$ by the definition of $a$. Also $\lVert l^\eta-l_0\rVert_2\to0$ as $\eta\downarrow0$, since $s(\eta)\to|L|$. [step 1.1, given, L2, L3, L4, algebra]

3.1 Let $l$ be the unique maximal solution with $l(0)=l^\eta$; it is defined for all $t\ge0$, because its invariant sphere $C=L^2$ is compact in $U$ and [L1] rules out breakdown inside a compact set. Let $\tau:=\inf\{t>0:l_1(t)\ge\delta_0\text{ or }l_1(t)\le0\}$, so $0<\tau\le+\infty$, and on $(0,\tau)$ one has $0<l_1<\delta_0$. On that interval $l_1(t)^2+l_3(t)^2\le l_1^2+a^2l_1^2<\delta_0^2(1+a^2)=L^2/4$ by [L2] (which gives $l_3=\pm al_1$ on the invariant level set $E=L^2/(2I_2)$, since $E-C/(2I_2)=0$ and $(1/I_2-1/I_3)>0$), so $l_2(t)^2=L^2-l_1^2-l_3^2>3L^2/4$ and $l_2$ has the constant sign $\sigma$ on $[0,\tau)$, its initial sign. Likewise $l_3=\pm al_1$ cannot change sign on $[0,\tau)$ without vanishing, which would force $l_1=l_3=0$ contrary to $l_1>0$; since $l_3(0)=-\sigma a\eta$, one has $l_3(t)=-\sigma al_1(t)$ there. [step 2.1, given, L1, L2, L4, algebra]

4.1 On $(0,\tau)$, the first component equation of [L2] and step 3.1 give $l_1'=(1/I_3-1/I_2)l_2l_3=a(1/I_2-1/I_3)(\sigma l_2)l_1\ \ge c_0l_1$ with $c_0=a(1/I_2-1/I_3)\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}|L|>0$, because $\sigma l_2\ge\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}|L|$. [step 3.1, L2, algebra]

5.1 By step 4.1 and the product and chain rules [L5], $\bigl(e^{-c_0t}l_1(t)\bigr)'=e^{-c_0t}(l_1'(t)-c_0l_1(t))\ge0$ on $(0,\tau)$; since $e^{-c_0t}l_1(t)$ is continuous on $[0,\tau)$, it is nondecreasing there by [L5], so $l_1(t)\ge\eta e^{c_0t}$ for $t\in[0,\tau)$. If $\tau=+\infty$, this would give $l_1(t)\ge\eta e^{c_0t}>\delta_0$ for $t>c_0^{-1}\log(\delta_0/\eta)$, contradicting $l_1<\delta_0$ on $(0,\tau)$; hence $\tau<+\infty$. [step 3.1, 4.1, given, L5, algebra]

6.1 At the time $\tau$ one has $l_1(\tau)=\delta_0$: indeed $l_1(\tau)\neq0$ by step 5.1 and continuity, so by the definition of $\tau$ and continuity it is the alternative $l_1(\tau)\ge\delta_0$ that occurs, and on $[0,\tau]$ the bound $l_1<\delta_0$ holds on $(0,\tau)$ with $l_1$ continuous, so $l_1(\tau)=\delta_0$; moreover $\tau\le c_0^{-1}\log(\delta_0/\eta)$. Therefore $\lVert l(\tau)-l_0\rVert_2^2\ge l_1(\tau)^2+l_3(\tau)^2=(1+a^2)\delta_0^2=L^2/4$, so $\lVert l(\tau)-l_0\rVert_2\ge |L|/2=\varepsilon_0$. [step 3.1, 5.1, given, L4, algebra]

7.1 It remains to make the initial point as close to $l_0$ as prescribed: for any $\delta>0$ choose $\eta>0$ with $\eta<\min\{\delta_0,\delta\}$ and $\lVert l^\eta-l_0\rVert_2<\delta$, possible because $\lVert l^\eta-l_0\rVert_2\to0$ by step 2.1. The corresponding solution then has $\lVert l(0)-l_0\rVert_2<\delta$ and, by step 6.1, escapes the ball of radius $\varepsilon_0$ at time $\tau\le c_0^{-1}\log(\delta_0/\eta)$. This is instability of $l_0$ in the sense of [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]], with the explicit time bound of the statement. [step 2.1, 6.1, given, algebra] ∎
